notes: Axis 'danger' = X (road conditions: clear 0 ↔ black ice 100). Axis 'speed' = Y (full stop 0 ↔ no limit 100). 'dir' = +1 when agreement moves the score toward the high end of its axis, -1 when agreement moves it toward the low end. 'type' = 'prob' (slider reads Very unlikely ↔ Very likely) or 'agree' (Strongly disagree ↔ Strongly agree). 'profile' items feed sub-scores only.

items.text: There is at least a 1-in-10 chance that advanced AI causes human extinction or permanently takes control away from humanity this century.
items.plain: The core question. Not 'will AI cause problems' but 'could it end us, or end our say over our own future'. One in ten is the bar: not certain, not negligible.
items.for: We are building minds that may outthink us, we can't yet verify what they want, and we only get one try. A 10% chance of the worst outcome is a conservative reading of that situation.
items.against: Every previous 'end of the world' technology story was wrong, today's systems show no sign of wanting anything, and a number like 10% is a guess dressed up as a probability.

items.text: We currently have no reliable way to check that a highly capable AI will behave as intended in situations its makers never tested.
items.plain: Can we look inside a model and know what it will do in a new situation? This asks whether that ability exists today.
items.for: Models are trained, not written. Interpretability research is young; labs test behavior by trying things, and a new situation is by definition not one of those things.
items.against: The same is true of every complex system, including people and companies, and we manage those with testing, monitoring and the ability to switch things off.

items.text: An AI could become far more capable than its makers expected, faster than they could react.
items.plain: The 'takeoff' question: could capability jump rather than climb, so that no one has time to adjust?
items.for: AI already helps build AI. Once systems improve the tools that improve them, progress can compound in months, not decades, and institutions move in years.
items.against: Progress has been steady and visible for a decade, limited by data, chips and money. Each generation takes years and billions; nothing about that looks like a sudden jump.

items.text: Today's AI is essentially a very good autocomplete, and this approach will stall well short of human-level general intelligence.
items.plain: Are large language models the road to general intelligence, or a dead end that looks impressive?
items.for: These systems predict text. They have no world model, no lasting memory, no goals, and they fail at simple reasoning in ways a child wouldn't. Scale has been hitting diminishing returns.
items.against: 'Just autocomplete' was said at every stage, and each stage did things the critics said it never would. Whatever the mechanism, the capabilities keep arriving.

items.text: If we build AI smarter than us, it will most likely end up pursuing goals we didn't intend.
items.plain: Not 'AI will hate us' but 'we won't manage to give it the goals we meant'. Would a smarter-than-human system end up wanting something else?
items.for: We don't know how to specify human values precisely, and training rewards what we can measure, not what we mean. Smarter systems find the gaps.
items.against: Current systems are trained on human text and feedback and come out broadly helpful. There is no evidence that intelligence brings alien goals with it; that's a story, not a finding.

items.text: The serious harms from AI in the next ten years will be things like scams, surveillance and job losses, not AI taking control.
items.plain: Where is the real damage? In the everyday harms already happening, or in a loss-of-control scenario?
items.for: Fraud, deepfakes, biased decisions and displaced workers are here now, hurting real people. Talk of superintelligence pulls attention and money away from them.
items.against: Both can be true, and the second kind is irreversible. Preparing for the harm you can't undo is not a distraction from the ones you can.

items.text: Humanity has handled dangerous technologies before, like nuclear weapons and biotech, and can handle AI the same way.
items.plain: We've built things that could kill millions and, so far, kept the lid on. Does that record transfer to AI?
items.for: Treaties, inspections, safety culture and plain self-interest have held for eighty years. AI is powerful, but it's still a technology made by people and institutions.
items.against: Nuclear weapons don't improve themselves, copy themselves or make decisions. And 'so far' includes several near-misses that came down to luck.

items.text: The most likely result of advanced AI is a world much better than today.
items.plain: Set aside the tail risks. Where does the middle of the distribution land: better, worse, or about the same?
items.for: Cheap intelligence means cheaper medicine, education, energy and science. Every general-purpose technology so far made life longer and richer, despite the fears.
items.against: 'Most likely' hides the question of who gets the gains and who bears the losses. Better on average can still mean worse for most people, and this time the tool may not stay a tool.

items.text: AI developers understand how their own systems work well enough to predict their behavior.
items.plain: Do the people building these models know what they've built?
items.for: They design the training, run thousands of evaluations, and ship systems used by hundreds of millions of people without disasters. That's what understanding looks like in practice.
items.against: The developers themselves say they can't explain why a model gives a particular answer. Evaluations catch what you thought to test for.

items.text: All work toward AI smarter than humans should stop until we know how to make it safe, even if that takes decades.
items.plain: The full-stop position: not slower, not more careful, but a halt on the path to superhuman AI until safety is solved.
items.for: You don't run an experiment that could kill everyone before you know how to run it safely. Decades of delay cost something; extinction costs everything.
items.against: A halt can't be verified, would be ignored by the least careful actors, and forfeits every benefit while solving nothing, since you learn safety by building.

items.text: The right response to AI risk is to build it faster, so the most careful developers get there first.
items.plain: The 'race to the top' argument: if powerful AI is coming anyway, better that the safety-minded reach it before the reckless.
items.for: The technology will be built by someone. The only lever you actually control is whether the people who care about safety are ahead or behind.
items.against: Everyone believes they are the careful one. Racing shortens the time to think, and the finish line is a system nobody knows how to control.

items.text: Governments should require a license before anyone trains an AI model above a certain size.
items.plain: Like a license for a nuclear plant or a new drug: permission before you build, not just rules after.
items.for: The largest training runs cost hundreds of millions and are done by a handful of firms; licensing them is feasible and puts a public check before the fact.
items.against: Licensing freezes the incumbents in place, invites capture, and regulates a number (model size) that stops meaning anything as methods improve.

items.text: There should be an international treaty limiting the largest AI training runs, enforced the way nuclear treaties are.
items.plain: A global agreement with inspections, so that no country or company can quietly race ahead.
items.for: The biggest runs need enormous chip clusters that can be counted and monitored. If the danger is global, the answer has to be too.
items.against: Treaties take decades, the rivals don't trust each other, and a limit on compute is a limit on a moving target. It would be broken quietly and enforced selectively.

items.text: A country that slows down its AI development mostly hands the advantage to countries that don't.
items.plain: The geopolitics argument: does unilateral caution just mean someone else wins?
items.for: AI leadership is economic and military leadership. Slowing down while rivals accelerate is not safety; it's surrender of the decision to people who care less.
items.against: The 'race' is mostly a story the racers tell. Capabilities diffuse in months anyway, and being first to an uncontrollable system is not a prize.

items.text: AI developers should have to show a model is safe before release, rather than regulators having to prove it's dangerous.
items.plain: Who carries the burden of proof: the builder (as with medicines) or the regulator (as with most software)?
items.for: When a product can cause harm at scale, the maker proves safety first. That's how aviation and pharmaceuticals earned public trust.
items.against: 'Prove it's safe' has no end point for a general technology. It becomes a veto held by whoever writes the test, and small players can't afford to pass it.

items.text: Existing laws on fraud, discrimination and product safety are enough; new AI-specific rules would do more harm than good.
items.plain: Do we need new laws for AI, or just to apply the ones we have?
items.for: Fraud is fraud whether a human or a model commits it. New rules written in a panic will be outdated in a year and protect incumbents, not people.
items.against: Existing law assumes a human actor and a slow pace. It has nothing to say about a system that can act on its own or a training run that can't be undone.

items.text: Slowing AI progress by a few years is acceptable if it meaningfully lowers the chance of catastrophe.
items.plain: The trade-off in one sentence. Would you pay a few years of delay for a real reduction in the worst-case risk?
items.for: A few years is nothing against the whole future. If waiting buys safety, it's the cheapest insurance ever offered.
items.against: 'A few years' is millions of preventable deaths from diseases we could have cured, and there is no guarantee the delay buys anything but a head start for others.

items.text: If a lab believed its next model had a 1% chance of causing a global catastrophe, it should not build it.
items.plain: One in a hundred. Is that an acceptable risk for a single product decision?
items.for: No engineer would launch a bridge with a 1% chance of collapse. A 1% chance of a global catastrophe is a thousand times worse and taken by a private company.
items.against: Every big decision carries risk, and not building has risks too. A 1% figure invented inside a lab is not a measurement; refusing to act on guesses is how nothing ever gets built.

items.text: Delaying AI by ten years would cost millions of lives, through slower medical and scientific progress.
items.plain: The cost of caution. Delay isn't free if AI would have found cures sooner.
items.for: AI is already accelerating drug discovery and diagnosis. Ten years of that, multiplied across the world's sick, is a body count we never see because it's counterfactual.
items.against: Medical progress is limited by trials, regulation and biology, not by a shortage of clever software. The lives-saved figure is a projection, not a fact.

items.text: Releasing the weights of the most powerful AI models openly does more good than harm.
items.plain: Open weights means anyone can download and run the model. Good for science and competition, or a gift to bad actors?
items.for: Openness is how we found and fixed the flaws in every other technology. Concentrating the strongest models in a few hands is the actual danger.
items.against: You can't recall an open model. Once the weights are out, every safeguard can be stripped by anyone, and the next generation may be capable of real damage.

items.text: Companies should be legally responsible for serious harm caused by their AI, as carmakers are for defective cars.
items.plain: Liability: if an AI system hurts someone, who pays?
items.for: Liability is what makes safety a business decision instead of a press release. Cars got safer when carmakers had to pay.
items.against: General-purpose tools are used in ways their makers can't foresee. Holding the toolmaker liable for every misuse ends open research and small companies.

items.text: I would trust a government agency more than an AI company to decide when a model is safe enough to release.
items.plain: Whom do you trust to make the call: the company that built it, or a public body?
items.for: Companies have a direct financial interest in shipping. A public agency answers, at least in principle, to everyone.
items.against: Agencies are slow, easily captured, and staffed by people who don't understand the technology. The company at least knows what it built.

items.text: Within 20 years, AI will do most of the thinking work humans are paid for today, better and cheaper.
items.plain: How big and how soon? This is about capability, not danger.
items.for: In five years we went from autocomplete to systems that write code, pass professional exams and run agents. Twenty more years of that is hard to imagine ending anywhere else.
items.against: Demos are not jobs. Most work involves bodies, trust, context and responsibility, and every automation wave has taken longer and gone less far than promised.

items.text: AI systems could someday deserve moral consideration, as animals do.
items.plain: Could there ever be something it is like to be an AI, so that how we treat it matters for its own sake?
items.for: We don't know what gives rise to experience. Systems that model themselves and their preferences may cross a line we won't notice we've crossed.
items.against: A program that says it suffers is a program that predicted those words. Extending moral status to software confuses imitation with life.

items.text: A few companies or governments controlling the most powerful AI is a bigger danger than AI acting on its own.
items.plain: Which do you fear more: the machine, or the people who own it?
items.for: Every past technology's harms came from who controlled it. Superhuman AI in a few hands is superhuman power in a few hands.
items.against: Concentration is a familiar problem with familiar remedies. A system that no one controls, including its owners, is a new one.
